topic.title: Agent2Agent protocol — discovery, tasks and artifacts

outcomes: Explain why A2A connects independent agents while MCP connects an AI host to tools and context.
Discover and validate an Agent Card, supported interfaces, skills, capabilities and security schemes.
Send messages and continue conversations using contextId and taskId.
Model asynchronous task states, artifacts, history, cancellation and authorization-required outcomes.
Consume streaming status/artifact events and configure secure push notifications.
prerequisites: Stage 7 MCP architecture, primitives, authorization and transports
HTTP, JSON-RPC, OAuth, asynchronous workflows and message schemas

glossary.definition: A machine-readable description of an agent's identity, endpoint interfaces, protocol versions, capabilities, skills, modalities and security schemes.
A named capability advertised by an agent with description, tags and examples.
An identifier grouping related messages and tasks into one conversation context.
An identifier for one asynchronous unit of agent work and its lifecycle.
A named output produced by a task, composed of one or more content parts.
A typed content block such as text, file or structured data.
A lifecycle status such as working, input-required, auth-required, completed, failed, canceled or rejected.
A server-to-client callback informing a registered endpoint about task status or artifact updates.

explanation.problem: A tool protocol is not enough when two independent agents need to delegate work, exchange messages, track long-running tasks and return artifacts. They may run in different organizations, use different models and have separate identity, memory and policy. A2A provides an interoperable agent-to-agent task and message protocol without requiring agents to expose their internal reasoning or tools.
explanation.plainLanguage:
MCP and A2A solve different integration problems. MCP lets an AI host connect to tools, resources and prompts. A2A lets one agent discover and delegate work to another independent agent. The calling agent does not need access to the remote agent's internal prompts, model, memory or tool implementations. It interacts through a public contract.

Discovery begins with an Agent Card, commonly published at /.well-known/agent-card.json. The card describes agent name and purpose, supported interfaces, protocol binding/version, capabilities such as streaming and push notifications, skills, input/output modes and security schemes. The client validates the card, selects a compatible interface and determines the authentication requirements before sending work. An Agent Card advertises capabilities; it is not a security authorization grant.

A2A messages carry a role and one or more typed parts. Parts can represent text, files or structured data. A message can belong to a context and can reference a task. A client sends a task request using message/send or message/stream. The server may return a direct message for quick work or a Task for asynchronous work. A Task has an id, contextId, status, status message, history and artifacts. The caller uses tasks/get to poll and tasks/cancel to request cancellation.

A context groups a multi-turn interaction; a task represents one unit of work. Do not confuse them. Multiple tasks may share a context, and a follow-up message may reference a previous task. The server must validate that the task and context belong together and that the caller is authorized to access them. IDs should be unguessable and scoped to tenant/user identity.

Task states communicate progress and control. Common states include submitted, working, input-required, auth-required, completed, failed, canceled and rejected. A task may pause because it needs more user input or authorization. Auth-required is a signal to complete the relevant authentication flow; it is not permission to bypass the security scheme. Cancellation is also a request, not proof that work stopped. The caller should read the resulting task state.

Artifacts are outputs. They have an artifact ID, optional name/description and one or more parts. A task may emit multiple artifacts or append chunks to one artifact. Streaming clients receive status updates and artifact updates, often through Server-Sent Events (SSE). A final event indicates completion. If streaming is unavailable, the client can poll tasks/get. Push notifications provide an alternative callback mechanism for long-running work; they require an authenticated, validated callback URL and delivery retries with idempotency.

A2A supports multiple protocol bindings, including JSON-RPC over HTTP, HTTP+JSON and gRPC. The Agent Card lists supported interfaces so the client can choose an interoperable binding. The transport does not remove the need for TLS, authentication, authorization, rate limits, request validation, task ownership checks and audit. The server must not leak task history or artifacts across tenants.

The remote agent is an independent trust domain. Its response may be incomplete, malicious or incorrect. Treat remote messages and artifacts as untrusted data, validate their type and size, preserve provenance and do not allow a remote agent to override local system policy. Give the remote agent only the minimum context needed. Avoid sending secrets or raw conversation history unless explicitly authorized. Apply timeouts, task quotas, cancellation and cost budgets.

Use A2A for delegation between agents and MCP for each agent's own tool/context integrations. A typical architecture has an orchestrator agent using A2A to delegate a refund review to a specialist agent; the specialist agent uses MCP to retrieve policy and order resources, then returns a task artifact to the orchestrator. Keep identities, credentials, scopes and audit trails separate across the two protocols.

Protocol-version discipline matters. The A2A project specification identifies 1.0.0 as the latest released specification in its release documentation at the time this lesson was prepared. Pin the protocol version and supported interface from the Agent Card; do not assume a development-branch schema is interchangeable with a released version. The protocol can be bound to JSON-RPC, HTTP+JSON or gRPC, while streaming and push notifications are capability-dependent. Check the official specification and SDK compatibility matrix before implementation.

Disambiguate ACP names: IBM/BeeAI's Agent Communication Protocol is historical agent-to-agent interoperability work; IBM Research now states that ACP has become part of A2A under the Linux Foundation. It is not the same protocol as the Agent Client Protocol used by IDEs and coding agents. This curriculum treats IBM ACP as a migration/history topic, and Agent Client Protocol as a separate client-to-agent protocol.
explanation.mentalModel: Discover Agent Card → select compatible interface → authenticate → send message/task → follow context/task state → receive artifacts → validate provenance and result.
limitations: An Agent Card describes capabilities but does not prove an agent is trustworthy or authorize access.
A task can be long-running; clients need polling, streaming or push notification handling.
Task cancellation may race with completion and is not guaranteed immediate.
Remote agent output is untrusted and may contain prompt injection or incorrect conclusions.
Context and task identifiers must be tenant scoped; guessing IDs must not reveal data.
A2A does not standardize the remote agent's internal reasoning, model or tools.
Do not confuse IBM/BeeAI Agent Communication Protocol with Agent Client Protocol for IDE integrations; their scopes and evolution differ.
explanation.everydayAnalogy: A project manager discovers a specialist through a service directory, assigns a job with a ticket number, tracks the ticket status and receives a deliverable. The specialist chooses its own tools and process; the manager only sees the agreed interface, status and artifact.
explanation.mathMadeSimple: An orchestrator sends one message and receives taskId=task-42 and contextId=ctx-9. It polls tasks/get every 5 seconds for at most 2 minutes, then times out or escalates. If the task emits 3 artifact updates, the client assembles them by artifactId and chunk metadata. The contextId groups the conversation; taskId identifies this one work item.
explanation.productionImpact: Production A2A needs validated Agent Cards, interface negotiation, OAuth or equivalent authentication, task/context ownership checks, bounded task history, streaming/polling/push fallback, artifact size and type validation, cancellation, idempotent callback delivery, provenance and cross-agent audit.

useCase.scenario: An orchestrator agent delegates refund eligibility review to a specialist agent. It discovers the specialist's Agent Card, authenticates, sends a message, follows the asynchronous task and receives a structured review artifact. The specialist uses its own MCP tools to read the policy and order; the orchestrator never receives its internal credentials.
constraints: Remote agent identity is authenticated and authorized.
Task/context IDs are scoped to tenant and caller.
Only minimum necessary data is shared.
Remote artifacts are untrusted and schema validated.
Cancellation and task state are read back from server.
MCP credentials remain inside specialist agent boundary.
outputs: Streaming status/artifact events or push notification
useCase.successMetric: The orchestrator delegates to a compatible specialist, tracks completion and consumes validated artifacts without sharing internal credentials or leaking tenant data.

components: SSE stream or push notification handler

dataFlow.purpose: Discover identity, interfaces, skills, capabilities and security schemes.
Persist task state and conversation continuity.
Retrieve evidence without exposing internal tools to orchestrator.

dataFlow.payload: SSE status/artifact events or push notification
dataFlow.purpose: Deliver task progress and final artifacts.

trustBoundaries: Agent Card is untrusted discovery data until validated and authenticated.
A2A auth is independent from MCP credentials used inside specialist agent.
Task/context lookup is tenant scoped and authorization checked.
Remote message/artifact content is untrusted and size/type limited.
Push callback URLs are validated against SSRF and DNS rebinding.
Audit records capture delegation, identity, task IDs and artifact provenance.
failurePaths: Unsupported protocol binding/version: reject before message dispatch.
Invalid Agent Card endpoint or mismatched identity: fail discovery.
Missing credentials: return auth-required and complete proper authentication.
Task/context mismatch: reject without exposing task existence.
Remote task times out: cancel if safe, otherwise mark unknown and reconcile.
Stream disconnect: resume through tasks/get or supported stream cursor.
Push callback fails: retry with bounded backoff and idempotent event ID.
Artifact contains unexpected MIME/type or oversized content: reject and quarantine.

failures.name: Agent Card spoofing
failures.symptom: Client sends private data to a lookalike agent endpoint.
failures.rootCause: Agent Card is trusted without validating its source, endpoint or security metadata.
failures.recovery: Use trusted discovery roots, HTTPS, identity checks and allow-listed domains.
failures.regressionTest: Mismatched Agent Card protocol/interface is rejected.

failures.name: Task/context confusion
failures.symptom: Follow-up message references task from another context or tenant.
failures.rootCause: Task and context IDs are not bound and authorization checked.
failures.recovery: Validate taskId/contextId pair and tenant ownership on every operation.
failures.regressionTest: Wrong context or tenant cannot read or continue task.

failures.name: Untrusted artifact
failures.symptom: Remote artifact contains malformed data or prompt injection.
failures.rootCause: Artifact content is consumed as trusted instructions.
failures.recovery: Validate MIME/schema/size, preserve provenance and treat as untrusted data.
failures.regressionTest: Invalid artifact is quarantined and not passed to privileged tools.

failures.name: Streaming disconnect
failures.symptom: Client loses task updates when SSE connection drops.
failures.rootCause: No polling fallback or resumable event cursor.
failures.recovery: Use tasks/get and supported stream resume semantics.
failures.regressionTest: Disconnect stream and retrieve latest task state by taskId.

failures.name: Push notification SSRF
failures.symptom: Remote agent posts callbacks to internal/private network address.
failures.rootCause: Callback URL is accepted without validation.
failures.recovery: Require HTTPS callback allow-list, DNS/IP validation and egress controls.
failures.regressionTest: Reject localhost, private IP and unapproved callback host.

Fetch and validate a specialist Agent Card.
Select JSON-RPC/HTTP+JSON/gRPC interface and check auth requirements.
Send a user message with minimum necessary context.
Render taskId, contextId, status and message history.

Request tasks/cancel and display actual terminal state.
Validate artifact MIME/schema/provenance before presenting it to user.

scenarioQuiz.question: What does A2A primarily connect?
options: A host to a local file
A database to a SQL client
A model to one tool schema
scenarioQuiz.explanation: A2A supports agent-to-agent discovery, task delegation and artifact exchange.

scenarioQuiz.question: What is the difference between contextId and taskId?
options: contextId groups conversation; taskId identifies one work item
contextId is an Agent Card version
scenarioQuiz.explanation: A context can contain multiple related tasks; each task has its own lifecycle.

scenarioQuiz.question: Does an Agent Card grant permission to call an agent?
options: No, authentication and authorization remain separate
scenarioQuiz.explanation: Agent Cards advertise interfaces and skills; callers still authenticate and authorize.

scenarioQuiz.question: A remote agent returns a completed artifact. What next?
scenarioQuiz.explanation: Remote artifacts are untrusted data and need validation before use.
